newsitem.title: UK: Britain to free bank fraudster wanted by U.S..
newsitem.headline: Britain to free bank fraudster wanted by U.S..

text.p: A key figure in the world's biggest banking fraud will be released from prison because the United States has failed to organise his extradition, Britain's High Court found on Tuesday.
Syed Ziauddin Ali Akbar, former treasury head at the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI), had waited long enough for his extradition to face blackmail charges, two judges ruled.
"The time has come to say enough is enough. He is discharged from custody forthwith," said Lord Justice Sir Christopher Rose.
Rose and his colleague Justice Maurice Kay gave lawyers working for the United States 24 hours to appeal the ruling.

Ali Akbar, 50, was sentenced to six years imprisonment in Britain in 1993 for his part in the $12 billion collapse of BCCI, after the Luxembourg-based bank was found to be operating a global money-laundering network.
He was released in August 1995, but rearrested immediately at the request of the United States and has been awaiting extradition in a south London prison since.
Under British law, anyone being held for extradition may appeal for release after two months.
Britain's Home Office (interior ministry) said it was up to the United States to make the case for Ali Akbar's extradition.
"It is now in the hands of the United States, it is not a matter for us," a spokesman said.
Ali Akbar's case has been complicated because France is objecting to his extradition to the United States.
The former BBCI treasurer fled to France in 1991 while on parole in Britain for a drug trafficking offence.
Paris agreed to extradite him to Britain to face trial for money laundering but is now objecting to his re-extradition to the U.S. to face a different set of charges, the Home Office spokesman said.
The collapse of BCCI left a quarter of a million creditors stranded around the world and shook the regulatory authorities that were accused of failing to spot its illegal activities.
The bank had assets of $24 billion and operations in 71 countries when it was shut down.
